abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Ovarian cancer (OC) is a lethal gynecologic malignancy, with modest responses to CPI. Engagement of additional immune arms, such as NK cells, may be of value. We focused on Siglec-7 as a surface antigen for engaging this population. Human antibodies against Siglec-7 were developed and characterized. Coculture of OC cells with PBMCs/NKs and Siglec-7 binding antibodies showed NK-mediated killing of OC lines. Anti–Siglec-7 mAb (DB7.2) enhanced survival in OC-challenged mice. In addition, the combination of DB7.2 and anti–PD-1 demonstrated further improved OC killing in vitro. To use Siglec-7 engagement as an OC-specific strategy, we engineered an NK cell engager (NKCE) to simultaneously engage NK cells through Siglec-7, and OC targets through FSHR. The NKCE demonstrated robust in vitro killing of FSHR+ OC, controlled tumors, and improved survival in OC-challenged mice. These studies support additional investigation of the Siglec-7 targeting approaches as important tools for OC and other recalcitrant cancers.
Anti-Siglec-7 MAb or Siglec-7 bispecific NK cell engager demonstrate potent targeted OC therapeutic activity in vitro and in vivo.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Ovarian cancer (OC) represents one of the most lethal gynecologic malignancies with more than 20,000 new diagnoses each year, resulting in more than 13,000 deaths annually in the United States alone (1). This high mortality and morbidity of OC can be largely attributed to its late-stage diagnosis along with high treatment resistance (2). Nearby 70% of the patients with high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) are diagnosed at an advanced stage of the disease and are associated with extremely poor outcomes (3). Despite advanced frontline treatments with surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy, the 5-year survival rate of OC is less than 25% for those diagnosed with stage III/IV disease. Although >80% of the patients exhibit initial response to therapy, disease recurrence occurs in the majority of patients (25% recurrence for patients with early-stage disease and >80% recurrence for patients with advanced disease), eventually leading to chemotherapy-resistant disease and progression (1, 2, 4). Immunotherapeutic strategies have also had limited success so far in the treatment of OC. Despite substantial rationale, immune checkpoint blockade using antibodies targeting programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) or programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) has shown limited efficacy in the treatment of epithelial OC, with a modest response rate of 4 to 15% (5). Likewise, in a phase 2 study in recurrent platinum-sensitive OC with Ipilimumab [human cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) monoclonal antibody (mAb)], the objective response rate was reported to be 10.3% (6).

Natural killer (NK) cells, a subset of lymphocytes comprising 5 to 20% of human peripheral blood lymphoid cells, may be an ideal tool to engage in this pursuit which are not yet fully engaged in immunotherapy of OC (7, 8). Different activities of NK cells, including their critical role in immunosurveillance, makes them attractive candidates for OC therapy (8). NK functions are regulated by multiple signals transmitted by the receptors present on the cell surface, which include both activating and inhibitory receptors (7, 9). One inhibitory receptor expressed on human NK cells is sialic acid (Sia)–binding immunoglobulin-like lectin-7 (Siglec-7) (7). It is described as a pan-NK marker due to its detected expression on both CD56dim (more cytotoxic) and CD56bright (more cytokine-producing immune regulatory) NK cell subsets, making it an important NK cell target (10, 11). Siglec-7 is believed to function as an inhibitory receptor in a ligand-Sia-binding–dependent manner (12). It is reported to exhibit preferential binding toward branched α(2,6)-linked Sia and α(2,8)-linked diSia, among others (13). Targeting OC is of particular importance since patients with OC are reported to have significantly enhanced level of the total sialylation (α2,3-/α2,6-linked Sia). The bi- and trisialylated highly branched glycans exhibit low expression in healthy individual, whereas they are reported to be overexpressed in patients with OC (14–16). The interaction between Siglec-7 and its ligands has been reported to play a role in the inhibition of NK-mediated antitumor toxicity (7). Accordingly, it appears to be an important receptor to target immune activating agents for enhancing NK-mediated antitumor immunity. We have developed a panel of mAbs against human Siglec-7. Here, we designed and studied fully humanized versions of strong Siglec-7 binders for their ability to enhance NK activity against ovarian tumors in model systems. We demonstrate that Siglec-7 blockade using these antibodies improved NK targeted function against OC tumor lines including those containing diverse cancer driver mutations as well as exhibiting high drug resistance phenotypes. In xCELLigence real-time cell analysis (RTCA), anti–Siglec-7 antibody (Ab) exhibited 10-fold higher potency than anti–PD-1 in side-by-side assays. In addition, dual treatment with both anti–PD-1 and anti–Siglec-7 displayed enhanced OC cell killing. DB7.2, a particular anti–Siglec-7 DNA-encoded mAb improved ovarian tumor control in humanized mice resulting in their enhanced survival in a lethal tumor challenge model. We hypothesized that the Siglec-7 binding could be used as a previously undescribed approach to target NK cells and developed a class of bispecific NK cell engager (NKCE) allowing for simultaneous targeting of Siglec-7 as well as a model OC antigen, follicle stimulating hormone receptor (FSHR), which we have recently reported (17). We characterized this new biologic and showed that the bispecific NKCE bound to both FSHR and Siglec-7 in vitro. The biologic was potent, with killing observed at pM levels against OC lines, in vitro. Furthermore, the bispecific NKCE could both shrink OC tumors and extend survival in an in vivo tumor therapy humanized animal model. These studies demonstrate the therapeutic potential of directly targeting OC by engagement and activation of NK cells using the Siglec-7 pathway, suggesting the possible importance of these approaches as new tools for potential treatment against recalcitrant malignant diseases.

sec.title: Siglec-7 mAbs exhibit in vitro expression and specificity
sec.p: To assess the potential for Siglec-7 blockade as an NK cell activation strategy, we generated codon and RNA-optimized Ab expression cassettes of potent Siglec-7 binders and assembled them into vectors optimized for production of human immunoglobulin G (IgG). Individual mAb combinations of the heavy chain (HC) and light chain (LC) are designated as DB7.1, DB7.2, and DB7.7 respectively (fig. S1A). Expression was studied in vitro by transfecting Expi293F cells with the synthetic human Siglec-7 DNA expression vectors to serve in Western blot analysis. These studies identify bands corresponding to the heavy and light chains of the expressed antibodies in the transfected Expi293F supernatant but not in the empty vector transfected control wells (fig. S1B). The in vitro expression of DB7.1, DB7.2, and DB7.7 was further confirmed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) quantification (fig. S1C). DB7.1, DB7.2, and DB7.7 Siglec-7 mAbs showed specific and dose-dependent binding to recombinant human Siglec-7 analyzed by ELISA (Fig. 1A). We stably transduced human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells for Siglec-7 expression and used those cells (HEK293T–Siglec-7 cells) for evaluation of binding by Siglec-7 mAbs. As shown in Fig. 1B, DB7.1, DB7.2, and DB7.7 showed specific binding to HEK293T–Siglec-7 cells. We also evaluated their binding to Siglec-9 for additional specificity. Siglec-7 and Siglec-9 are closely related exhibiting high sequence similarity (18). Notably, we did not obverse any binding of DB7.1, DB7.2, and DB7.7 to Siglec-9–transduced HEK293T cells (HEK293T–Siglec-9 cells), confirming the specificity of the Siglec-7 mAbs (fig. S1D). The most potent binder DB7.2 was further analyzed for reactivity against peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from multiple donors (n = 4) (fig. S2). DB7.2 bound predominantly to human NK cells (~90%), whereas lower levels of reactivity were observed in the case of CD8+ T and CD4+ T cells (Fig. 1, C and D). We document binding of DB7.2 to innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) (~13%) which may be considered as the innate counterparts of CD4+ T helper 1 (TH1), TH2, and TH17 cells (19). In addition, DB7.2 showed binding to a mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cell subpopulation. MAIT cells are reported to play important role in immune defense against microbial infections in mucosal barriers and serve as innate sensors of inflammation and viral infection (20, 21). Additional analyses of the more minor T cell populations that express Siglec-7 are important for further study. DB7.2 mAb stained both CD56dim and CD56bright NK cell subsets, suggesting its ability to bind the bulk of human NK populations (Fig. 1E). DB7.2 also demonstrated strong binding to human Siglec-7 protein in Western blot analysis (fig. S3A). We also studied the binding affinity using surface plasmon resonance (SPR). DB7.2 exhibited a KD value of 44 pM as determined using a titration of different concentrations of anti–Siglec-7. Besides demonstrating high affinity, DB7.2 was specific since it did not bind to irrelevant negative control protein at concentrations up to 200 nM in the SPR assay (fig. S3, B to D).

sec.title: Siglec-7 mAbs induced potent and specific killing of target OC cells in vitro
sec.p: To evaluate the Siglec-7 genetically optimized mAbs ability to activate human peripheral blood NK cells against human cancer lines, we assembled a diverse panel of human OC cells (table S1) (17), using HaCaT (human keratinocyte cells) as negative control. HaCaT cells do not express Siglec-7 ligands in contrast to different OC cells evaluated (fig. S4). DB7.1, DB7.2, and DB7.7 did not induce killing of HaCaT cells (Fig. 2, A and B). We next examined the ability of the mAbs to drive killing of defined human OC cells (OVCAR10, OVISE-FSHR, PEO4, and TOV-21G) with different disease phenotypes and mutations (table S1) in the presence of human PBMCs/NK cells. While all three clones induced killing of OC targets (Fig. 2, C to G), we did not observe killing in the no Ab control [effector + target (E + T)] (Fig. 2, C to G) or irrelevant Ab control/isotype control (fig. S5, A and B). Clone DB7.2 exhibited the highest potency in these assays. DB7.2 displayed enhanced killing induction against two additional OC lines, CaOV3 (fig. S5C) and OVCAR3 (fig. S5D) cells. In addition, DB7.2 induced significant killing of OVCAR10, PEO4, and OVCAR3-FSHR cells in the presence of purified NK cells as effector component, whereas no killing was observed in the case of no Ab control or isotype control (Fig. 2, H and I, and fig. S5E).

sec.p: To confirm Siglec-7 mAb activities independence from Fc receptor binding (fig. S6A), we observed that DB7.2 potency was maintained in the presence of Fc blockade (fig. S6B). We next performed residue modification of the Fc of the antibodies to eliminate Fc engagement and potential off-target effects. We designed a variant of DB7.2 which contains multiple residue modifications (“TM”; L234F/L235E/P331S) in the Fc domain to ablate FcR and complement (C1q) binding (22, 23), designated as DB7.2_TM Mod. The killing efficacy of DB7.2_TM Mod was maintained in OVISE-FSHR cells (Fig. 3A). Post–24-hour addition of DB7.2_TM Mod to OVISE-FSHR cells in the presence of human PBMCs demonstrated potent killing of target cells, when compared to no Ab control cells (Fig. 3B). DB7.2 and DB7.2_TM Mod exhibited comparable median effective concentration (EC50) values of 82.67 and 192 nM, respectively, against OVISE-FSHR cells (Fig. 3, C and D). Together, these studies illustrate the Siglec-7 mAbs’ specificity for activating immune killing and ability to target OC cells.

sec.title: Combination of anti PD-1 with DB7.2 mAb demonstrates enhancement of OC killing using xCELLigence assay
sec.p: OC is one of the subsets of cancers with modest responses to existing immune checkpoint blockade therapy. Patients with OC receiving checkpoint inhibitors (CPIs) also generated infrequent durable responses (24). However, evidence suggests that combinatorial methods might prove important to optimize OC patient response to immunotherapy (25, 26). We hypothesized that the combination of T cell activating PD-1 with activation of NK cells by Siglec-7 mAb could target tumors more efficiently. To test this hypothesis for simultaneous targeting of PD-1 (for T cells) and Siglec-7 (for engaging NK immune pathways), we have performed a preliminary study of the combinations of DB7.2 and anti–PD-1 (Pembrolizumab) in xCELLigence RTCA targeting PEO4 cells. PEO4 cells express both PD-L1 (fig. S7) and Siglec-7 ligands (fig. S4). DB7.2 showed the ability to kill breast cancer 2 (BRCA2)-mutated and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi)–resistant PEO4 cells with an EC50 68.87 nM (Fig. 3, E and G), whereas anti–PD-1–targeted PEO4 cells with a 10× higher EC50 680 nM (Fig. 3, F and H) in xCELLigence-based in vitro killing assays. The combination of anti PD-1 (T cell CPI) with DB7.2 showed significant enhancement of PEO4 cell killing in the presence of human PBMCs when compared to individual treatments (Fig. 3I). These initial datasets show that the combination of anti–Siglec-7 and anti–PD-1–enhanced antitumor immunity, supporting that additional studies are important to further extend this observation.

sec.title: In vivo expression of Siglec-7 mAbs reduces tumor progression in an OC-challenged model
sec.p: We next developed expression cassettes to study the effects of the anti–Siglec-7 mAb clones in vivo. To that end, we injected mice with DNA expression cassettes for the mAb (27) at a dose of 50 μg + 50 μg (HC + LC) in a two-plasmid system designed for each anti–Siglec-7 clone (DB7.1, DB7.2, and DB7.7) along with empty vector control (pVax1) allowing for biologic Ab production in vivo. Injections were performed into the tibialis anterior muscle of mice on day 0 as previously described (Fig. 4A) (23, 27). The presence of human IgG in sera from the DB7.1, DB7.2, and DB7.7 Siglec-7 mAb-injected mice was observed, and no expression was detected in control animals or in the prebleed mouse sera. To confirm the specificity of the in vivo–generated antibodies, we stained human NK cells using day 14 sera obtained from mice inoculated with either DB7.1, DB7.2, or DB7.7 versus sera from empty vector control delivered animals. Day 14 sera from all the three groups positively stained human NK cells, whereas staining was not observed in the case of pVax1 or irrelevant Ab controls (Fig. 4B).

sec.p: To examine the antitumor potency of Siglec-7 mAb delivery in animals, we used an NSG-K (NOD/SCID- γ-MHC I/II double-knockout mutant) mouse tumor challenge model in which we injected OVISE-FSHR human OC cells (0.8 × 106 cells per mouse) and monitored tumor growth prospectively. When the tumor became palpable, we delivered 50 μg + 50 μg (HC + LC) of DB7.2 DmAb or pVax1 vector control in the muscle as described (23, 27) together with 10 million human PBMCs per mouse (Fig. 4C). Mice receiving DB7.2 Siglec-7 DmAb exhibited a significant decrease in the tumor burden/delay in tumor growth compared to the vector control (Fig. 4D and fig. S8, A and B). Notably, the Siglec-7 DmAb enhanced the median survival of tumor bearing mice (Fig. 4E). A second study using a different PBMC donor also showed DB7.2 DmAb to significantly attenuate tumor burden in OVISE-challenged NSG-K mice when compared to irrelevant DmAb control (fig. S9). PBMCs injected to the mice had no background effect on the growth of tumor in OVISE-challenged model (fig. S10). These in vivo data support the potential of Siglec-7 antibodies in treatment of OC.

sec.title: DB7.2xD2AP11 DNA-encoded bispecific NKCE exhibits in vitro expression and binding to Siglec-7 and FSHR
sec.p: NK engagers are an important new focus for targeting tumor cells (18, 28, 29). On the basis of the potency of the anti Siglec-7 mAbs to enhance NK activity against OC, we considered the potential of this molecule as specific NKCE approach. We hypothesized that this approach would not only allow for specific targeting of NK cells but also prevent NK cells from receiving negative tumor immune microenvironment signals, resulting in a previously undescribed NKCE concept. Therefore, to enhance targeting tumors using NK cell–specific Siglec-7 engagement, we constructed a NKCE in the format of two linked single-chain variable fragments (scFVs) arranged to bind to the OC antigen FSHR as recently described (17) and anti–Siglec-7 FV. We designed DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE fusion sequence encoding the scFV of DB7.2 anti–Siglec-7 Ab with the scFV of anti-FSHR (clone D2AP11) (Fig. 5A) (17) incorporating a GS (glycine-serine) flexible linker (30, 31). In vitro analysis showed the NKCE was efficiently expressed, through transfection of Expi293F cells, we observed production of an expected ~55-kDa molecule (Fig. 5B). We demonstrated that this NKCE binds to both cellular targets by flow staining on Siglec-7 or FSHR overexpressing HEK293T (Fig. 5C) or K562 (Fig. 5D) cells, respectively. To visualize the binding to human Siglec-7, high-resolution confocal imaging of 293T–Siglec-7 fixed cells were performed. Cells were labeled with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI; nuclei), green fluorescent protein (GFP; Siglec-7), and Texas Red (DB7.2xD2AP11). DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE demonstrated clear surface binding to GFP+ cells expressing human Siglec-7 but not in the secondary Ab control (Fig.5E).

sec.title: FSHR-targeted NKCE induces potent killing in multiple ovarian tumor lines and decreases tumor burden in vivo
sec.p: Next, we evaluated the DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE for induction of tumor killing in vitro using the xCelligence RTCA assay. The effector cells studied include either PBMCs or donor NK cells directly added into the cultures. The NKCE and effector cells were added a day after the plating of target OC cells. As controls, we studied four FSHR-negative cell lines, including HEK293T cells (32), AGS human gastric cancer cells, GM05389 human fibroblast cells, and WM3743 human melanoma cells. We did not observe off-target killing against these FSHR-negative cells (Fig. 5, F to K) including irrelevant cancer cells. As shown in Fig. 5 (G and J), HEK293T and AGS cells remained healthy and adherent through 2 to 3 days of treatment with DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE in the presence of human PMBCs. In contrast, multiple FSHR expressing ovarian tumor lines OVISE, OVCAR3-FSHR, CaOV3, Kuramochi-FSHR, and PEO4 (Fig. 6, A to G) were efficiently killed by human PBMCs in the presence of DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE. As an additional specificity control, we studied directly adding purified human NK cells as effector cells. DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE coincubated with human NK cells also effectively killed OVCAR3-FSHR cells (fig. S11A). Notably, D2AP11-TCE (a bispecific T cell engager targeting FSHR; FSHRxCD3) (17) did not induce killing of OVCAR3-FSHR and PEO4 cells in the presence of purified NK cells, indicating the importance of the Siglec-7 arm in NK-mediated target cell killing in this experiment (fig. S11, B and C). As a further specificity control, we developed a non-FSHR targeting NKCE; IL13Rα2-NKCE (NKCE targeting IL13Rα2) (31) and observed that it did not drive toxicity in FSHR overexpressing OVCAR3 or against OVISE cells (fig. S11, D and E). DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE induced concentration-dependent cytolysis in both OVISE-FSHR (human PBMCs from three different donors) and OVCAR3 cells showing EC50 values of 142.87 and 236.6 pM respectively, supporting the potency of this engager tool for targeting pathogenic cells as a previously undescribed NKCE (Fig. 6, H and I, and figs. 12 and 13). We examined the induction of cytotoxic molecule secretion profiles of the OC-NKCE. Coculture of OVCAR3-FSHR cells and human PBMCs and DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE (Fig. 7A) generated enhanced production of soluble Fas (sFas) and granzyme A as part of the specific immune activation, with decreased levels of interleukin-10 (IL-10) observed, compared to no Ab control groups (Fig. 7B), supporting a more effector-based activation. Similar profiles were observed when PEO4 cells were cocultured with purified NK cells in the presence of DB7.2xD2AP11. DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE led to enhanced production of sFas and granzyme A and decreased IL-10 level when compared to irrelevant NKCE (fig. S14).

DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE significantly decreased the tumor burden and enhanced the survival of OVCAR3-FSHR tumor–bearing mice.

sec.p: To directly evaluate the in vivo antitumor effects of DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE, we challenged NSG-K mice with OVCAR3-FSHR cells. NSG-K mice were administered 3 million OVCAR3-FSHR cells and 7 days after tumor implantation, they were treated for in vivo expression using DNA-encoded DB7.2xD2AP11NKCE (100 μg) or empty vector; pVax1 (100 μg), twice, three weeks apart. On the same day, the animals were also inoculated with 10 million human PBMCs, and tumor volumes were measured periodically (Fig. 7C). Therapy with the NKCE led to the significantly decreased tumor burden in OVCAR3-FSHR tumor–bearing mice, while no such impact was observed in the control treated group (Fig. 7D). Further, DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE treatment significantly enhanced the survival of the OC-challenged mice compared to the control group (Fig. 7E). The in vivo antitumor effects of DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE were further evaluated in Nu/J mice challenged with OVISE cells. We observed that DB7.2xD2AP11 in the presence of human PBMCs was able to significantly decrease the tumor burden in this model (fig. S15), supporting further studies of this approach.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Aggressive OC types such as HGSC and ovarian carcinosarcoma are referred to as “Cold” tumors as they exhibit low tissue infiltrating lymphocytes and are associated with poor treatment responses (33, 34). Thus, engaging immune responses by additional means are important for immune targeting of cold tumors (8). The innate immune effector system is important to consider as NK cells serve as a first line of defense in tumor immunosurveillance (35). Tumors evade the T cell responses through multiple mechanisms such as major histocompatibility complex (MHC) downmodulation and up-regulation of T cell exhaustion programs (36). Similarly, cancers can use host systems to bypass the surveillance function of NK cells through immune evasion strategies including shedding soluble ligands for NK activating receptors, release of inhibitory cytokines, up-regulation of human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecules, and thus escape NK immune function (37), but NK nonresponsiveness is also likely mediated by additional NK regulatory pathways. Recent studies have identified that many tumors display increased levels of Sia on their surface, which likely function as a negative or blocking signal to NK cells allowing the tumor to avoid NK immune surveillance (38). One effort in the approach to strengthen NK activation against such hypersialylated tumors is the desialylation of target cells expressing ligands of Siglec-7 (11). As NK cells display Siglec-7, a receptor/sensor for distinct sialoglycan determinants, which when engaged on the surface of human NK cells through tumor association can serve to inhibit NK-mediated target killing (39–41). These may exhibit regulatory negative signals by a sialoglycan tumor shield. Very recent studies suggest that some Siglecs could function as glyco-immune switch molecules that inhibit NK-mediated antitumor immunity in an MHC-independent manner (42). Bertozi and group demonstrated a glycocalyx editing approach using Ab-enzyme conjugates. These chemically fused recombinant sialidase linked to trastuzumab (Ab-sialidase conjugate) resulted in desialylation of cancer cells in a HER2-dependent fashion, which improved binding to NKG2D (NK-activating receptor NK group 2D) and also augmented antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) against cancer cells with moderate HER2 expression (43). In a syngeneic orthotopic HER2+ breast cancer mouse model, treatment with another sialoglycan degrader, trastuzumab-sialidase conjugate 2, delayed tumor growth, increased infiltration of immune cells, and extended survival of mice in trastuzumab-resistant breast cancer (44). In this study, we sought to investigate the use of mAbs or derivatives that target Siglec-7 directly and allow for tumor immune modulation and to extend and improve potential glyco-targeted immune function to improve the ability to target and impact tumor control.

Our group has designed different immunogens and developed several antibodies against disease targets (17, 23, 45, 46). Here, we aimed to augment antitumor immune responses for aggressive and difficult to treat OC. In this study, we focused on three highly potent Siglec-7 binding clones. These antibodies were engineered as human IgG1, and their immune cell binding was studied. We observed strong staining of anti–Siglec-7 Ab on NK cells including both bright and dim NK subsets suggesting its ability to bind bulk effector NK population. These human Siglec-7 antibodies drive NK immune function facilitating specific killing of target OC cells. This approach should be relatively agnostic to tumor mutations. We tested OC lines with multiple genetic mutations including BRCA1, BRCA2, AKT2, tumor protein p53 (TP53), Speckle-Type Poz Protein (SPOP), signal transducers and activators of transcription 3 (STAT3), mammalian target of rapamycin (MTOR), mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase-1 (MEK1), mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase-2 (MEK2), and v-raf murine sarcoma viral oncogene homolog B1 (BRAF), among others (table S1), and we observed that all lines with the escape mutations were targeted by anti–Siglec-7 antibodies resulting in the antitumor immune activation of NK cell targets. We hypothesized that these activities might be complementary to traditional PD-1 CPI approaches. Accordingly, we studied anti–Siglec-7 mAb in combination with anti–PD-1 CPI. From our initial dataset, we found that the dual treatment exhibited improved antitumor effects, suggesting additional investigation. In addition, we observed that the potency of the anti–Siglec-7 Ab was greater than the anti–PD-1 Ab, Pembrolizumab, against PEO4 cells, suggesting the potential value of the combined NK T cell approach. We next used a humanized NSG mouse model engrafted with human PBMCs and observed that a single dose of encoded DB7.2 Siglec-7 mAb was sufficient to generate notable tumor control and increase the median survival of mice bearing human ovarian tumors. Because of a limitation of the NSG model in that it will develop graft versus host disease (47) over a few months, only single dose of anti–Siglec-7 was administered, yet it was still effective. This suggests that additional treatment using multiple doses over time, as current CPIs are clinically used (48), could be studied.

We further sought to focus on the potency of Siglec-7 binding and activation of NK cells for targeted OC therapy. We hypothesized that binding to Siglec-7 could directly engage NK cells and draw them to a cell target in an efficient manner without driving a negative immune signal. We developed and characterized a type of NKCE by creating a bispecific fusion between FSHR targeting mAb and a potent anti–Siglec-7 mAb. NKCEs have emerged as an interesting innate immune concept in the field of immune oncology. One such bispecific which has been advanced into the clinic; GTB-3550 engaging CD16a-IL-15/CD33 for AML and CD33+ malignancies. Other NK targets being studied preclinically include NKG2D, NKp30, and NKp46 (18, 28, 29). Ibarlucea-Benitez et al. (18) showed that Fc engineered Siglec-7 and Siglec-9 antibodies reduced tumor burden in Siglec-7/9/Siglec-E knockout mice. The phenotype shown for our anti–Siglec-7 mAbs of binding and activation of NK cells that would otherwise be negatively affected by a tumor sialoglycan cloak suggest that Siglec-7 could provide a unique immune tool for specific tumor-NK activation and engagement. The bispecific DB7.2xD2AP11, exhibited binding to both NK cells and OC cells. It displayed killing (pM level) against diverse OC phenotypes. To the best of our knowledge, this study demostrates a previously undescribed bispecific NKCE approach using Siglec-7 or any member of the Siglec family . This NKCE was specific for its target cells and potent in tumor cell killing, as evaluated using a panel of different human ovarian tumor lines. FSHR expression on targets was a requirement for NK killing activity, as FSHR-negative cells were not killed. DB7.2xD2AP11 led to fewer cytotoxic molecules being produced compared to conventional T cell engager, suggesting its importance to study as a killing tool with a potential limited risk of cytokine release syndrome (49). In addition, the NKCE was highly potent in controlling tumor burden in vivo in OVCAR3-FSHR/OVISE–challenged mouse models in the presence of human PBMCs.

During these studies, we focused on OC cells that express mutations that are particularly problematic for OC therapies. This included PARPi-resistant OC cells and OC displaying resistance against diverse drug targets, specifically histone deacetylase (Dacinostat, Entinostat, and Belinostat), phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) (Dactolisib and Buparlisib), mammalian target of rapamycin complex (mTORC) (Omipalisib), Wee1 (CHEK1), Ttopoisomerase 1 (TOP1) (Gallibiscoquinazole, Mitoxantrone, and Irinotecan), DNA alkylating agents (Oxaliplatin and Cisplatin), and microtubule stabilizer (Docetaxel) (table S1) (50–55). Our studies included OC lines containing BRCA (BRCA1 and BRCA2) mutations as these are a major risk in OC cancer patient cohorts. Around 50% of HGSCs exhibit disrupted BRCA pathway either via germline or somatic mutation or through epigenetic silencing of pathway members (3). PARP inhibition represents an important pathway for DNA damage repair, and therefore, PARPi holds great promise for the treatment of tumors with disruptive mutations in BRCA1/2. However, resistance to PARPi has been reported to be a problem for treating resistant patients with OC (56). The potency and consistency for killing FSHR+ tumors using both the Siglec-7 mAb as well as the bispecific Siglec-7 NKCE in vitro and in vivo are encouraging for potentially bringing additional tools to treat poorly responding OCs.

In summary, these studies describe the development of Siglec-7 mAbs that engage and activate NK cells and may complement PD-1 against difficult cancers representing a potential additional class of molecule for NK cell engagement. We describe that Siglec-7 can be used to design an interesting NKCE that functions as a tool for targeting receptor-positive tumors driving notable antitumor responses in vitro and in vivo. While these studies are important for designing potential tools for OC, other studies are warranted to examine the utility of such biologics against additional difficult to treat cancers.

sec.title: Cells and animals
sec.p: OVCAR3, CaOV3, and TOV-21G cells were provided by J. R. Conejo-Garcia (Department of Immunology, Moffitt Cancer Center, Tampa, Florida). OVISE, OVCAR10, PEO4, and Kuramochi cells were provided by R. Zhang (The Wistar Institute). HaCaT human keratinocyte and WM3743 melanoma cells were provided by M. Herlyn (The Wistar Institute). HEK293T, Expi293F, and AGS gastric cancer and GM05389 human fibroblast cells were obtained from American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). 293T cells were transduced retrovirally to express Siglec-7/Siglec-9; OVCAR3, OVISE, and Kuramochi cells were retrovirally transduced with human FSHR as described previously (57, 58). K562 cells were purchased from ATCC and retrovirally transduced to express FSHR. Human PBMCs/NK cells from healthy donors were provided by the Human Immunology Core of the University of Pennsylvania.
Balb/c and Nu/J mice were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory. NSG-K (NSG-MHC I/II double-knockout mutant) mice were purchased from The Wistar Institute Animal Facility.

sec.title: DNA-encoded mAb generation
sec.p: The HC and LC sequences of anti–Siglec-7 clones were used to develop Siglec-7 DNA-encoded monoclonal antibodies (DmAbs) as tools for in vitro expression (27). Final human IgG1 HC and LC were inserted into a pVax1 plasmid expression vector, under the control of the human cytomegalovirus promoter and bovine growth hormone polyadenylation signal as described (27). Plasmids were then transfected into Expi293F cells using the Expifectamine 293 expression Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to produce antibodies. The purity and apparent molecular weight of the antibodies were assessed by SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis analysis.

sec.title: Design of FSHRx Siglec-7 NKCE
sec.p: FSHRxSiglec-7 NKCE was designed by encoding a codon-optimized scFv of anti–Siglec-7 mAb (DB7.2) followed by the scFv of anti-FSHR Ab (D2AP11) with the addition of an enhancing optimized IgE leader sequence. Both constructs were subcloned into a modified pVax1 expression vector (17, 30, 59). FSHRxSiglec-7 NKCE is designated as DB7.2xD2AP11.

sec.title: Flow cytometry
sec.p: We used a BD LSRII flow cytometer for staining of cells. BD FACS Aria cell sorter (BD Biosciences) was used for the sorting of Siglec-7/Siglec-9/FSHR stably expressing cells. Antihuman antibodies used were directly fluorochrome-conjugated. We used anti–Siglec-7 (clone F023-420, BD Pharmingen) and anti–Siglec-9 (clone K8, BioLegend). For the nonconjugated primary antibodies, phycoerythrin (PE) secondary antihuman (H + L) (Invitrogen) and PE/AF647 secondary antihuman F(ab′)2 (Jackson ImmunoResearch Laboratories Inc.) were used. A Live/Dead Violet viability kit (Invitrogen) was used to exclude dead cells from analysis.

For fluorescence cytometry staining on PBMCs, the following antibodies were used: CD69 PE-Cy5 (clone FN50), PD-1 BV421 (clone EH12.2H7), CCR7 APC-Cy7 (G043H7), CD19 BV785 (clone HIB19), CD27 BV650 (clone 0323), CD56 BV570 (clone HCD56), CD16 BV711 (clone 3G8), CD21 PE-Cy7 (clone BU32), and Siglec-7 (clone 6-434) from BioLegend; CD11c BUV395 (clone B-ly6), CXCR5 BV750 (clone RF8B2), CD3 BUV805 (UCHT1), CD45 AF700 (clone HI30), CD127 PE-CF594 (clone HIL-7R-M21), CD25 BUV737 (clone 2A3), CD8 BUV496 (clone RPA-T8), HLA-DR BV605 (clone G46-6), CD38 BUV661 (clone HIT2), CD14 BV480 (clone MP9), CD45RA BUV563 (HI100), CD4 BB790 (clone SK3), CD15 FITC (clone HI98), CD103 BB700 (clone Ber-ACT8), and CD161 APC (clone DX12) from BD Biosciences. Briefly, cryopreserved PBMCs were thawed and rested for 2 hours at 37°C and 5% CO2 in complete R10 media [RPMI supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, 2 mM l-glutamine, penicillin (100 U/ml), and streptomycin (100 mg/ml)] with deoxyribonuclease I (10 U/ml; Roche Life Sciences). Cells were washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and incubated with DB7.2 anti–Siglec-7 Ab diluted in fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) buffer for 20 min. After washing with FACS buffer, cells were incubated with mouse antihuman IgG Fab secondary Ab PE (Invitrogen) diluted in FACS buffer for 20 min. Cells were washed with FACS buffer, resuspended in PBS, and prestained for chemokine receptor CCR7 and CXCR5 for 10 min at 37°C 5% CO2. Then, cells were stained for viability exclusion using Live/Dead Fixable Aqua (Invitrogen) for 10 min, followed by a 20-min incubation with a panel of directly conjugated mAbs and Human TruStain FcX (BioLegend), diluted in equal parts of FACS buffer (PBS containing 0.1% sodium azide and 1% bovine serum albumin) and brilliant stain buffer (BD Biosciences). Stained cells were washed and fixed in PBS containing 1% paraformaldehyde (Sigma-Aldrich). Samples were acquired using a FACS Symphony A5 cytometer, and analysis was performed by FlowJo software 10.8.1 (Tree Star Inc.). Binding of DB7.2 to the indicated gated cell populations was detected using PE mouse antihuman IgG Fab secondary Ab (Invitrogen). Commercial anti–Siglec-7 (clone 6-434) from BioLegend was used in parallel.

For detection of Siglec-7 ligand expression, cells (5 × 105) were first incubated with fixable viability dye eFluor780 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 15 min. Cells were then incubated with recombinant human Siglec-7/CD328 Fc chimera protein (R&D Systems) for 30 min followed by staining with PE-conjugated goat antihuman IgG Fc secondary Ab (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 30 min. Sample acquisition and analysis were done using a BD LSRII flow cytometer and FlowJo software.

sec.title: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
sec.p: For quantification of human IgGs in Siglec-7 mAbs as well as Siglec-7 DmAb electroporated mouse sera, MaxiSorp plates were coated at 4°C overnight with goat-anti human IgG Fc (10 μg/ml; Bethyl). Plates were washed and blocked with 5% milk in PBS-T (0.05% Tween 20 in PBS) for 2 hours at room temperature (RT). Plates were washed, and samples diluted in 1% newborn calf serum (NCS) in PBS containing 0.2% Tween 20 were added and incubated at 37°C for 2 hours. Plates were again washed and incubated with 1:10,000 dilution of horseradish peroxidase–conjugated goat antihuman IgG (H + L) secondary Ab (Bethyl) for 1 hour at RT. The plates were developed with SigmaFast OPD for 5 to 10 min, and optical density at 450 nm signals were measured.

sec.title: In vitro cytotoxicity analysis using xCELLigence real-time cell analyzer
sec.p: In vitro cytotoxicity analysis was performed using xCELLigence RTCA equipment, Agilent Technologies, USA, as described (17). Disposable sterile 96-well E-plates of the xCELLigence RTCA device were used for seeding the target cells (1 × 104 to 2 × 104 cells per well). After 18 to 24 hours of incubation, the effector cells (E) and treatments (Siglec-7 mAbs/NKCE) were added to the target cells (T); E(PBMC):T = 5:1/10:1; E (NK):T = 3:1. The data generated were normalized and analyzed as previously described (17).

sec.title: Western blot analysis
sec.p: For validating the in vitro and in vivo expression of Siglec-7 mAbs, the supernatant collected after transfection of Expi293F cells with the DNA encoding antibodies or sera collected from mice after inoculating with the Siglec-7 DmAbs were heat-inactivated, reduced, and loaded with Odyssey Protein Molecular Weight (LI-COR). Following electrophoresis, samples were transferred onto polyvinylidene fluoride membranes via an iBlot-2 system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and blocked using Odyssey Blocking Buffer (LI-COR). The HC and LC were detected using goat antihuman secondary Ab (LI-COR). The expression of bispecific NKCE was detected using goat antihuman IgG F(ab′)2 (Jackson ImmunoResearch Laboratories Inc.) followed by donkey anti-goat Ab (LI-COR). To detect the binding of DB7.2 to Siglec-7 (ACROBiosystems), goat antihuman secondary Ab (LI-COR) was used.

sec.title: SPR analysis of the binding affinity
sec.p: The binding affinity of DB7.2 to Siglec-7 was evaluated using Biacore T200 SPR system. DB7.2 was immobilized on a protein A/G chip. Siglec-7 (ACROBiosystems) was diluted in running buffer [10 mM Hepes (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, and 0.1% Tween 20] to different concentrations; 3.125 to 200 nM, 1:2 dilutions, was tested at flow rate 30 μl/min. After each injection, the DB7.2/Siglec-7 complex was removed from the chip with a 60-s injection of 20 mM glycine (pH 2.0), followed by the capture of fresh DB7.2. The KD value for DB7.2 was determined by nonlinear regression fits of the association and dissociation curves at each concentration using biacore T200 evaluation software. Binding of irrelevant Ab to Siglec-7 or irrelevant protein was detected in parallel.

sec.title: Immunofluorescence analysis
sec.p: Siglec-7–transduced HEK293T cells were seeded in two-well chamber slides and allowed the cells to adhere overnight. The cells were permeabilized using 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS followed by blocking using 5% goat serum. Following this, bispecific NKCE was added and incubated overnight at 4°C. Subsequently, the slides were incubated with goat antihuman H + L (Texas Red conjugated) secondary antibodies. Nuclear staining was done with DAPI. The samples were mounted onto glass slides with the help of Fluoroshield mounting medium (Invitrogen) and then observed using a Leica TCS SP8 WLL scanning laser confocal microscope.

sec.title: Analysis of cytotoxic molecule secretion profile
sec.p: OVCAR3-FSHR/PEO4 (1 × 104 cells per well) were plated (96-well plate) and incubated overnight. PBMCs (E:T = 10:1) or NK cells (E:T = 3:1) and treatments (DB7.2xD2AP11-NKCE, pVax1 or irrelevant NKCE) were then added to the target cells. After 72 hours, the supernatants were analyzed for secreted cytotoxic molecules by Human CD8/NK Panel bead-based assay (BioLegend) following the manufacturer’s instructions.

sec.title: Tumor challenges
sec.p: NSG-K (NOD/SCID- γ-MHC I/II double-knockout mutant) mice were challenged with OVISE-FSHR/OVISE cells (0.8 × 106/1 × 106 per mouse) on the right flank subcutaneously. When the tumor became palpable, mice were inoculated with DB7.2 DmAb (50 μg +50 μg; HC + LC), pVax1 (100 μg), or irrelevant DmAb (50 μg + 50 μg; HC + LC) followed by intraperitoneal injection of 10 × 106 PBMCs into each mouse. Tumor sizes of the mice were measured periodically. Tumor volume (V) was calculated as per the formula V = (length × width2)/2; width is the side with smaller measurement. Mice were euthanized upon exceeding 20-mm size (any side) or developing signs of graft-versus-host disease. For the DB7.2xD2AP11 NKCE study, we challenged NSG-K mice with OVCAR3-FSHR cells (3 × 106 per mouse). When the tumor became palpable, mice were inoculated with pVax1 (100 μg) or DB7.2xD2AP11 (100 μg). The same day when expression vector was given, we injected 10 × 106 PBMCs intraperitoneally into each mouse. The mice were inoculated with DNA twice, 3 weeks apart. Tumor volumes and survival of mice were calculated following the same procedure as described. In addition, we challenged Nu/J mice with OVISE cells (1 × 106 per mouse). When the tumor became palpable, mice were inoculated with pVax1 (100 μg) or DB7.2xD2AP11 (100 μg) followed by intraperitoneal injection of PBMCs (10 × 106 per mouse), and tumor sizes were monitored periodically. Animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at The Wistar Institute.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were done using GraphPad Prism. A P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant, *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, and ****P < 0.0001. Differences between the means of experimental groups were calculated using Student’s t test or one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) where more than two quantitative variables were measured. Error bars represent SEM/SD. Comparison of normalized cell index in the xCelligence RTCA or comparison between tumor sizes at each time point was done using two-way ANOVA.
